SECTIONS.title: Anatomical terms, planes and axes
ideas: Every description starts from anatomical position: standing upright, facing forward, arms at the sides with palms forward. Directions: superior/inferior, anterior/posterior, medial/lateral, proximal/distal (along a limb) and superficial/deep.

Each cardinal plane pairs with the axis that pierces it at a right angle. Sagittal plane + mediolateral axis: flexion and extension, dorsiflexion and plantarflexion. Frontal (coronal) plane + anteroposterior axis: abduction and adduction, lateral flexion, radial and ulnar deviation. Transverse plane + longitudinal (vertical) axis: medial and lateral rotation, pronation and supination, horizontal abduction and adduction.

Special movements: circumduction (a cone combining several planes), protraction/retraction and elevation/depression (scapula, mandible), upward/downward rotation (scapula), opposition (thumb), inversion/eversion and the triplanar pronation/supination of the foot.

Kinematics describes motion (angles, velocity) without its causes; kinetics studies the forces and torques that cause it. Osteokinematics is the motion of bones through planes; arthrokinematics is motion between joint surfaces (roll, glide, spin).

Degrees of freedom are the planes a joint can move in: hinge 1, condyloid and saddle 2, ball-and-socket 3. In an open kinetic chain the distal segment moves freely (a seated leg extension); in a closed chain it is fixed and the proximal segment moves over it (a squat).

SECTIONS.title: Joint structure and arthrokinematics
ideas: Structural classes: fibrous (sutures, the distal tibiofibular syndesmosis, gomphoses), cartilaginous (symphyses such as the pubic symphysis and intervertebral discs; synchondroses such as growth plates) and synovial (with a joint cavity). Functional classes: synarthrosis (immovable), amphiarthrosis (slightly movable), diarthrosis (freely movable).
A synovial joint has hyaline articular cartilage, a capsule (fibrous outer layer, synovial membrane inside), synovial fluid and ligaments; many add menisci or discs, a labrum, bursae or fat pads.

Six synovial types: plane (intercarpal, AC), hinge (humeroulnar, interphalangeal), pivot (proximal radioulnar, atlantoaxial), condyloid (radiocarpal, MCP), saddle (thumb CMC) and ball-and-socket (glenohumeral, hip).

Arthrokinematics: surfaces roll, glide (slide) and spin. The convex–concave rule: when a convex surface moves on a fixed concave one, it rolls and glides in opposite directions; when a concave surface moves on a fixed convex one, they go the same direction.

The close-packed position has maximal congruence and taut ligaments: most stable, least joint play (knee in full extension, glenohumeral in abduction with lateral rotation, humeroulnar in extension). The loose-packed (resting) position has the most play. Mobility and stability trade off: the shallow shoulder moves more than the deep hip.

SECTIONS.title: Connective tissue and muscle mechanics
ideas: Tissues are loaded in tension, compression, shear, bending and torsion. Stress = force ÷ area and strain = change in length ÷ original length. A stress–strain curve has a toe region (crimp straightening), an elastic region, a plastic region (permanent deformation) and failure; the slope is stiffness.

Connective tissues are viscoelastic: creep (lengthening under a constant load), stress relaxation (falling stress at a constant length) and rate dependence. Ligaments join bone to bone and tendons muscle to bone (dense, parallel collagen); cartilage resists compression; bone remodels to the loads it carries (Wolff’s law), and disuse weakens every tissue.

Muscle architecture: parallel (fusiform) fibers, as in sartorius and biceps, favor range and speed; pennate fibers (unipennate, bipennate such as rectus femoris, multipennate such as deltoid) pack in more fibers, raising the physiological cross-sectional area and therefore force.

Length–tension: active force peaks near resting length, where actin and myosin overlap best; passive tension rises with stretch. Force–velocity: concentric force drops as speed rises, and eccentric force can exceed maximal isometric force. Active insufficiency: a two-joint muscle shortened across both joints produces little force (a weak fist with the wrist flexed). Passive insufficiency: a two-joint muscle cannot stretch across both joints at once (hamstrings limit hip flexion with the knee straight).

Contraction types: concentric (shortening), eccentric (lengthening under load, controlling a lowering) and isometric (no length change). Roles: agonist (prime mover), antagonist, synergist, stabilizer and neutralizer. When gravity drives a motion, the muscle on the opposite side controls it eccentrically.

SECTIONS.title: Levers, torque and biomechanics
ideas: Torque (moment of force) = force × the perpendicular distance from the axis to the force’s line of action (the moment arm). Units: N·m. A muscle or load makes the most torque when it acts at right angles to the segment.

Levers are named by what sits in the middle. First class: axis in the middle (nodding the head at the atlanto-occipital joint; triceps pulling on the olecranon). Second class: resistance in the middle (a wheelbarrow; rising onto the toes is the usual body example). Third class: effort in the middle (biceps at the elbow and most limb muscles).

Mechanical advantage = effort arm ÷ resistance arm. Above 1 (second class) favors force; below 1 (third class) favors speed and range of motion. Muscles attach close to joints, so they must pull with forces many times the load but move the hand or foot fast and far.

Static equilibrium: the forces and torques on a segment each sum to zero. To hold a load still, muscle force × muscle moment arm = load × load moment arm (plus the segment’s own weight × its moment arm).

Newton’s laws: inertia, F = ma, and action–reaction (the ground reaction force). A muscle’s pull splits into a rotary component (perpendicular, making torque) and a stabilizing or dislocating component (along the bone), and the split changes with joint angle. A low center of gravity over a wide base of support is more stable.

SECTIONS.title: The axial skeleton: vertebral column
ideas: The column has 7 cervical, 12 thoracic and 5 lumbar vertebrae, the sacrum (5 fused) and the coccyx (about 4 fused). Curves: cervical and lumbar lordosis (secondary curves, developing with head control and walking) and thoracic and sacral kyphosis (primary curves, present at birth).

A typical vertebra: a body for weight bearing; a vertebral arch (pedicles and laminae) around the vertebral foramen; spinous and transverse processes; and superior and inferior articular processes that form the facet (zygapophyseal) joints. Cervical: transverse foramina, bifid spinous processes. Thoracic: costal facets for ribs, long downward spines. Lumbar: large bodies, short square spines.
The atlas (C1) has no body: the atlanto-occipital joint nods “yes” (flexion and extension). The axis (C2) has the dens: the atlantoaxial joint turns “no” and provides about half of cervical rotation.

The intervertebral disc has a gel nucleus pulposus inside a ring of collagen layers, the annulus fibrosus. Flexion pushes the nucleus posteriorly, which is why disc herniations are usually posterolateral, toward the nerve roots.

Facet orientation sets each region’s motion: cervical facets allow all motions, especially rotation; thoracic facets allow rotation and lateral flexion but the ribs limit them; lumbar facets lie near the sagittal plane, favoring flexion and extension and blocking rotation. Ligaments: anterior longitudinal (limits extension), posterior longitudinal and ligamentum flavum (limit flexion; the flavum is elastic), interspinous, supraspinous and the nuchal ligament.

SECTIONS.title: Trunk muscles, posture and spinal cord injury
ideas: Abdominals: rectus abdominis (trunk flexion, posterior pelvic tilt), external oblique (rotation to the opposite side), internal oblique (rotation to the same side) and transversus abdominis (compresses the abdomen and stiffens the spine without moving it).

Back and neck: erector spinae (iliocostalis, longissimus, spinalis: extension and lateral flexion), transversospinalis (multifidus for segmental stability, rotatores, semispinalis), quadratus lumborum (lateral flexion, hip hiking), sternocleidomastoid (both sides: neck flexion; one side: lateral flexion toward and rotation away), scalenes and splenius muscles.

Deep “core” muscles (transversus abdominis, multifidus, diaphragm, pelvic floor) stiffen the spine; superficial muscles move it. Posture deviations: excess kyphosis, excess lordosis (often with anterior pelvic tilt), flat back, forward head and scoliosis (a lateral curve with vertebral rotation).

The spinal cord ends near L1–L2 (conus medullaris); below it is the cauda equina. There are 31 pairs of spinal nerves: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral and 1 coccygeal. C1–C7 exit above their vertebra, C8 below C7, and the rest below theirs.

Spinal cord injury: the level and completeness (ASIA A–E) set what function remains. Injuries at C3–C5 threaten breathing (“C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive”). Cervical injuries cause tetraplegia; thoracic or lower, paraplegia. Key muscles: C5 elbow flexors, C6 wrist extensors, C7 elbow extensors, C8 finger flexors, T1 little-finger abductors; L2 hip flexors, L3 knee extensors, L4 ankle dorsiflexors, L5 long toe extensors, S1 ankle plantarflexors.

SECTIONS.title: The shoulder complex
ideas: Four joints: sternoclavicular (saddle; the only bony link between the arm and the trunk), acromioclavicular (plane), glenohumeral (ball-and-socket) and the scapulothoracic articulation (a functional joint, not a true one).

The glenohumeral joint trades stability for mobility: a shallow glenoid deepened by the labrum, a loose capsule with superior, middle and inferior glenohumeral ligaments, and the rotator cuff, SITS: supraspinatus (starts abduction), infraspinatus and teres minor (lateral rotation) and subscapularis (medial rotation), which press the head into the socket. Most dislocations are anterior-inferior.

Scapulohumeral rhythm: about 2° of glenohumeral motion for every 1° of scapular upward rotation, so 180° of elevation is about 120° glenohumeral + 60° scapulothoracic. The upper and lower trapezius and serratus anterior form the upward-rotation force couple; the clavicle elevates and rotates posteriorly, and the humerus must rotate laterally to clear the greater tubercle.

Scapular muscles: trapezius (upper: elevation, upward rotation; middle: retraction; lower: depression, upward rotation), rhomboids (retraction, downward rotation), levator scapulae (elevation, downward rotation), serratus anterior (protraction, upward rotation; long thoracic nerve, or the scapula “wings”) and pectoralis minor.

Arm movers: deltoid (anterior: flexion and medial rotation; middle: abduction; posterior: extension and lateral rotation; axillary nerve), pectoralis major (adduction, medial rotation, flexion), latissimus dorsi (extension, adduction, medial rotation; thoracodorsal nerve), teres major and coracobrachialis. Subacromial impingement pinches the supraspinatus tendon and bursa under the acromion.

SECTIONS.title: Elbow and forearm
ideas: The elbow complex: humeroulnar (hinge; trochlea in the trochlear notch; the main flexion–extension joint), humeroradial (capitulum with the radial head; flexion–extension plus spin) and proximal radioulnar (pivot; the radial head turns in the annular ligament). The distal radioulnar joint completes pronation and supination, and the interosseous membrane passes force from radius to ulna.

The carrying angle is a normal valgus of about 10–15° (often a bit more in females). The ulnar (medial) collateral ligament resists valgus stress and is injured in throwing; the radial (lateral) collateral resists varus; the annular ligament holds the radial head (a pulled “nursemaid’s elbow” in young children).

Flexors: brachialis (a pure flexor on the ulna, working in any forearm position), biceps brachii (flexion and the strongest supination, best with the elbow at 90°) and brachioradialis (strongest in the thumb-up midposition). Extensors: triceps brachii (the long head also extends the shoulder) and anconeus.

Pronators: pronator quadratus (the main one) and pronator teres. Supinators: supinator and biceps. Normal range: about 0–150° flexion, 80° pronation, 80° supination; the humeroulnar joint is close-packed in extension.

Nerves: musculocutaneous (biceps, brachialis, coracobrachialis), radial (triceps, brachioradialis, supinator, wrist and finger extensors), median (pronators, most wrist and finger flexors), ulnar (flexor carpi ulnaris, part of FDP, most hand intrinsics). Lateral epicondylitis (“tennis elbow”) involves the common extensor origin; medial epicondylitis (“golfer’s elbow”) the flexor–pronator origin.

SECTIONS.title: Wrist and hand
ideas: Carpals, lateral to medial. Proximal row: scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform. Distal row: trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate. The scaphoid is the most often fractured (a fall on an outstretched hand, with snuffbox tenderness and a risk of avascular necrosis); the lunate is the most often dislocated.

The wrist is the radiocarpal joint (condyloid: radius with scaphoid and lunate; the ulna is separated by the triangular fibrocartilage complex) plus the midcarpal joints. Normal range: about 80° flexion, 70° extension, 20° radial and 30° ulnar deviation.

Wrist flexors start on the medial epicondyle (flexor carpi radialis, flexor carpi ulnaris, palmaris longus); extensors on the lateral epicondyle (extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis, extensor carpi ulnaris). Radial deviation pairs a radial flexor and extensor; ulnar deviation pairs FCU and ECU. Wrist extensors stabilize the wrist for a strong grip.

Extrinsic finger muscles: flexor digitorum superficialis (flexes the PIP), flexor digitorum profundus (the only DIP flexor) and extensor digitorum; the thumb has FPL, EPL, EPB and APL (the snuffbox borders). Intrinsics: thenar muscles (median nerve), hypothenar muscles, lumbricals (flex the MCPs and extend the IPs) and interossei (PAD: palmar adduct; DAB: dorsal abduct; ulnar nerve).

The thumb CMC is a saddle joint that allows opposition. The carpal tunnel holds nine tendons (4 FDS, 4 FDP, FPL) and the median nerve; compression numbs the thumb to the radial ring finger and weakens the thenar muscles. Grips: power (cylindrical, spherical, hook) and precision (pad-to-pad, tip-to-tip, lateral pinch). Nerve injuries: radial, wrist drop; ulnar, claw hand; median, “ape hand.”

SECTIONS.title: Pelvis, sacroiliac joint and hip
ideas: The pelvis: two hip bones (ilium, ischium and pubis, fused at the acetabulum), the sacrum and the coccyx. The sacroiliac joint is very stable with small motions, nutation (the sacral base tips forward) and counternutation, held by strong sacroiliac, sacrotuberous and sacrospinous ligaments.

Pelvic tilt: anterior tilt (ASIS forward and down) increases lumbar lordosis and flexes the hip; posterior tilt flattens the lumbar spine. Lumbopelvic rhythm pairs trunk flexion with hip flexion when you bend forward.

The hip is a deep ball-and-socket with a labrum. The femoral angle of inclination is about 125° in adults (smaller: coxa vara; larger: coxa valga) and anteversion about 15° (excess causes in-toeing). Ligaments: iliofemoral (the Y ligament, strongest, limits extension), pubofemoral and ischiofemoral. Close-packed: extension with medial rotation and abduction.

Muscles. Flexors: iliopsoas, rectus femoris, sartorius, TFL, pectineus. Extensors: gluteus maximus (climbing, rising) and the hamstrings. Abductors: gluteus medius and minimus, TFL. Adductors: adductor longus, brevis and magnus, gracilis, pectineus. Lateral rotators: piriformis, gemelli, obturators, quadratus femoris and gluteus maximus.

In single-leg stance the stance-side gluteus medius keeps the pelvis level; if it is weak, the opposite side drops: a Trendelenburg sign. A cane goes in the hand opposite the painful hip. Nerves: femoral (quadriceps, iliacus), obturator (adductors), superior gluteal (gluteus medius and minimus, TFL), inferior gluteal (gluteus maximus), sciatic (hamstrings).

SECTIONS.title: The knee
ideas: The tibiofemoral joint is a modified hinge: about 135° of flexion, plus rotation when the knee is bent. The menisci deepen the surface and absorb load: the medial one is C-shaped and attached to the MCL (less mobile, more often torn); the lateral one is more circular and mobile. At the patellofemoral joint, the patella (a sesamoid bone) lengthens the quadriceps’ moment arm.

Ligaments: ACL (stops the tibia sliding forward on the femur; injured in noncontact cutting and landing), PCL (stops posterior sliding; “dashboard” injuries), MCL (resists valgus) and LCL (resists varus). A blow to the outside of the knee can cause the “unhappy triad”: ACL, MCL and medial meniscus.

The screw-home mechanism: in the last 20–30° of extension the tibia rotates laterally on the femur (or, standing, the femur rotates medially on the tibia), locking the knee in its close-packed position. The popliteus unlocks it.
Convex–concave at the knee: in open-chain extension the concave tibia rolls and glides anteriorly (same direction). Rising from a squat, the convex femur rolls anteriorly and glides posteriorly.

Muscles: quadriceps (rectus femoris, which also flexes the hip, and the three vasti; femoral nerve), hamstrings (knee flexion and hip extension; sciatic nerve), gastrocnemius, popliteus, and the pes anserinus (sartorius, gracilis, semitendinosus). The Q-angle (ASIS to mid-patella to tibial tuberosity) is about 10–15°, and larger angles pull the patella laterally.

SECTIONS.title: Leg and ankle
ideas: The talocrural (ankle) joint is a hinge between the talus and the mortise formed by the tibia and fibula: about 20° dorsiflexion and 50° plantarflexion. The talus is wider in front, so the joint is close-packed and most stable in dorsiflexion; sprains happen in plantarflexion with inversion.

The subtalar joint (talus on calcaneus) provides most inversion (about 35°) and eversion (about 15°). Open-chain pronation = dorsiflexion + eversion + abduction; supination = plantarflexion + inversion + adduction.

Lateral ligaments: anterior talofibular (the most often sprained), calcaneofibular and posterior talofibular. The medial deltoid ligament is so strong that eversion injuries often break bone instead. A “high ankle sprain” injures the distal tibiofibular syndesmosis.

Compartments. Anterior (tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis longus, extensor digitorum longus): dorsiflexion, deep fibular nerve. Lateral (fibularis longus and brevis): eversion, superficial fibular nerve. Superficial posterior (gastrocnemius, soleus, plantaris, joining in the Achilles tendon): plantarflexion, tibial nerve. Deep posterior (tibialis posterior, FDL, FHL, “Tom, Dick and Harry” behind the medial malleolus): inversion and plantarflexion.

The gastrocnemius crosses the knee, so it is strongest with the knee straight; the soleus crosses only the ankle and dominates with the knee bent. Tibialis anterior lowers the foot eccentrically after heel contact; if it is weak (common fibular nerve injury at the fibular head), the foot slaps or drops. Other problems: Achilles tendinopathy or rupture, medial tibial stress syndrome and compartment syndrome.

SECTIONS.title: The foot
ideas: 26 bones: 7 tarsals (talus, calcaneus, navicular, cuboid and three cuneiforms), 5 metatarsals and 14 phalanges. Regions: rearfoot (talus, calcaneus), midfoot (navicular, cuboid, cuneiforms) and forefoot (metatarsals, phalanges).

The transverse tarsal (midtarsal) joint, talonavicular plus calcaneocuboid, works with the subtalar joint: pronated and unlocked, the foot is a flexible adapter at contact; supinated and locked, it is a rigid lever for push-off.

Three arches: medial longitudinal (the highest), lateral longitudinal and transverse. They are held by bone shape, the plantar fascia, the spring ligament (plantar calcaneonavicular), the long and short plantar ligaments, and muscles (tibialis posterior, fibularis longus, the intrinsics).

The windlass mechanism: extending the toes at push-off winds the plantar fascia around the metatarsal heads, raising the arch and stiffening the foot. Plantar fasciitis causes heel pain at the fascia’s origin, worst with the first steps of the morning.

Foot types: pes planus (flat, often overpronated) and pes cavus (high, rigid, poor shock absorption). Other problems: hallux valgus (bunion), hammer toes, metatarsal stress fractures and Morton’s neuroma (usually between the third and fourth metatarsal heads). The intrinsic muscles lie in four plantar layers and support the arch.

SECTIONS.title: Gait
ideas: A gait cycle (one stride) runs from one foot’s initial contact to that same foot’s next contact; a step is from one foot’s contact to the other’s. At normal walking speed, stance ≈ 60% and swing ≈ 40% of the cycle, with two double-support periods of about 10% each.

Stance phases (Rancho Los Amigos): initial contact, loading response, midstance, terminal stance and preswing. Swing: initial swing, midswing and terminal swing. Older terms: heel strike, foot flat, midstance, heel off and toe off.

Muscles: in loading response, tibialis anterior lowers the foot and the quadriceps control knee flexion (both eccentric), gluteus maximus and the hamstrings extend the hip and gluteus medius steadies the pelvis. From midstance, the calf controls the tibia moving forward, then pushes off. In swing, the hip flexors advance the leg, the dorsiflexors clear the toes and the hamstrings slow the leg in terminal swing.

Typical walking ranges: the knee flexes about 15–20° in loading response and about 60° in swing; the ankle reaches about 10° dorsiflexion in stance and 15–20° plantarflexion at toe-off; the hip moves from about 30° flexion at contact to about 10° extension in terminal stance.

Walking speed = step length × cadence. Running adds a flight phase and loses double support, and stance falls below half the cycle. Deviations: Trendelenburg gait (weak gluteus medius), foot slap or steppage gait (weak dorsiflexors), antalgic gait (short stance on a painful leg), backward trunk lean (weak gluteus maximus) and circumduction or vaulting (a functionally long leg).
